title: ENVIRONMENTAL PREFERENCE: A Comparison of Four Domains of Predictors
research_question: To compare the effectiveness of four domains of environmental attributes (Physical Attributes, Land Cover types, Informational variables, and Perception-based variables) in predicting environmental preference, and to assess the relative ability of variables within each domain to predict scenic quality or preference in a particular setting.

participants.description: Students enrolled in introductory psychology courses at the University of Michigan (n=88) and Grand Valley State College (n=92).
participants.recruitment: Students enrolled in introductory psychology courses

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 59 color slides of small forested areas, agricultural land, and fields in Scio Township, Washtenaw County, Michigan, with little topographic variation. Excluded residential, commercial, industrial, rivers, and lakes.

measures.instrument: 5-point Likert scale ('how much they like the kinds of places that are shown in the slides')
7 variables (Slope/relief, Edge contrast, Spatial diversity, Naturalism, Compatibility, Height contrast, Variety) rated on a 5-point scale by two research assistants
6 variables (Agriculture, Cut Grassland, Weedy Field, Scrubland, Forests, Woodlawn) rated as binary (presence/absence) by two research assistants
4 variables (Coherence, Complexity, Legibility, Mystery) rated on a 5-point scale by a panel of five individuals (authors and research assistants)
3 variables (Openness, Smoothness, Locomotion) rated on a 5-point scale by two research assistants

findings.antecedent: All 20 predictor variables (Physical Attributes, Land Cover types, Informational variables, Perception-based variables)
findings.quote: Regression analysis based on all 20 independent variables (combining across the four domains) accounted for a substantial amount of variance (R2 = .83; adjusted R2 = .75).

findings.mechanism: Preference is enhanced by the relative absence of the attribute.
Mystery emphasizes an inferential process and the importance of a search for information, leading to positive preference.
Preference is enhanced by the relative absence of the attribute. Most 'open' scenes were agricultural areas or weedy fields with little on which to focus attention.
Smooth ground texture enhances preference, possibly by suggesting ease of movement or processing fluency.
Preference is enhanced by the relative absence of the attribute.

findings.antecedent: Land Cover types domain (Agriculture, Cut Grassland, Weedy Field, Scrubland, Forests, Woodlawn)

findings.mechanism: Agriculture is a significant negative aspect in participants' preferences.
Weedy Fields are a significant negative aspect in participants' preferences.
Scrubland is a significant negative aspect in participants' preferences.

findings.antecedent: Informational Variables domain (Coherence, Complexity, Legibility, Mystery)

findings.mechanism: Mystery is a positive predictor of preference in natural settings, consistent with previous findings.
Openness was a negative predictor, suggesting that less open scenes were preferred, possibly due to lack of focus or perceived safety.
Smooth ground texture enhances preference, likely by suggesting ease of movement and processing fluency.
Ease of traversing without undue effort contributes to preference.

findings.antecedent: Physical Attributes domain (Slope/relief, Edge contrast, Spatial diversity, Naturalism, Compatibility, Height contrast, Variety)
findings.mechanism: The study area had very little topographic variation, limiting the test of landform predictors. Few scenes included anything but vegetation, limiting tests for Compatibility and Naturalism.
Scenes showing more variation were somewhat preferred.

mechanisms: The perceptual process involves extracting information from one's environment, with spatial organization providing information about how one could function in it (Informational Variables).
Rapid, unconscious decisions about ease of movement in a space affect preference (Perception-based Variables).
Preference is enhanced by the relative absence of attributes like Weedy Fields, Scrubland, and Openness, and by the presence of Mystery and Smoothness.
implementation_implications: Visual resource management should recognize environmental attributes salient to scenic quality, considering different predictor domains.
The ease of measuring a characteristic is important, but readily measurable attributes from spatial data banks are not necessarily the most useful for understanding scenic quality.
Future studies should sample predictors more widely, as different domains offer independent predictive power.
The effectiveness of certain predictor types may vary across different environmental contexts, suggesting a need for environmental sampling and categorization.

tables.description: Multiple-Regression Analysis Summary Results for Landcover, Informational, Perceptual, and Physical predictor domains, including partial correlation (r), regression coefficient (coef.), standard error (stand. error), F-statistic (F), p-value (p), and first-order correlation of preference and attribute (a).

limitations: The ratio of scenes (59) to predictors (20) is quite small, requiring caution in interpreting results.
Land Cover types were based on binary ratings, while other variables used five-point scales.
Some variables were highly interrelated (e.g., Perception-based and Informational variables).
Inter-rater reliabilities were not computed for predictor variables, and data sheets were misplaced.
The study area had very little topographic variation, limiting the test of landform predictors.
Very few scenes included anything but vegetation, limiting the test of Compatibility and Naturalism.
The failure of Coherence to reach significance remains unexplained.
The conceptualization of Legibility is still not completely satisfactory.
It is not yet clear whether characteristics most useful for understanding scenic quality can be readily derived from spatial data sources.

paper_metadata.title: Environmental Preference
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This article examines four domains of variables to assess their relative merit in explaining environmental preference. Within each of the domains, between three and seven specific attributes were measured, for a total of 20 predictor variables. The study site includes small forested areas, agricultural land, and fields, with little topographic variation. Preference ratings of 59 scenes representing the area serve as the dependent variable. Taken together, the 20 attributes accounted for 83 percent of the preference variance. Taken separately, the Physical Attributes lacked predictive power. Of the Informational variables, Mystery was the only significant contributor. The Land Cover types proved effective, with Weedy Fields, Scrubland, and Agriculture all significant negative predictors. Finally, the Perception-based variables were most powerful, with Openness and Smoothness particularly useful predictors. The results point to the importance of using different predictor domains, rather than relying exclusively on any one, since their role in different environmental contexts is likely to vary.
